seoTitle: Birthday Paradox & Hash Collision Probability Calculator
metaDescription: Compute the probability that at least two of n items collide among N possible values (birthdays, IDs, truncated hashes) and how many items give 50% or 1 in a million.
intro: Find out how soon random identifiers or hashes will start to collide.
why:
Enter the number of items and the size of the space (a number such as 365 or 2^64). For small spaces the exact product is used; otherwise the standard approximation 1 - e^(-n(n-1)/(2N)). The page also gives the number of items for a 50%, 1% and one-in-a-million collision chance.

The birthday bound means a b-bit random value starts colliding after roughly 2^(b/2) items, which is why short hash prefixes and 64-bit IDs need care. Results assume uniformly random values.

No data is sent anywhere: the work happens in your browser, so you can use it offline once the page has loaded.
howTo: Check the item counts for common risk levels.
Use more bits if the risk is too high.

faq.a: Because the number of pairs grows with the square of the group size.

faq.q: How many bits for 1 billion IDs?
faq.a: To keep collision chance near 1 in a million you need about 70 bits.

faq.q: Does it apply to hash functions?
faq.a: Yes for random outputs. It describes accidental collisions, not attacks.
No. Everything is processed in your browser, and the page makes no network requests with your input.
